extracted.intended_audience: NLP / HCI / creative-writing researchers, model developers, and evaluators interested in automated and expert assessment of short fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the Torrance Test for Creative Writing (TTCW) to evaluate short fictional stories across a battery of binary tests (14 dimensions) with expert justifications; also studying LLMs as assessors. Focus is on short fiction quality (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration, rhetorical complexity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understandability & Coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: A Fluency test assessing whether the story is understandable and coherent throughout (literal coherence and sense-making).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts flagged contradictions, parts that do not make sense, and random/incoherent elements (e.g., characters acting inconsistently across the story). Passing requires clarity of meaning and internal consistency; failures include nonsensical passages, abrupt unrelated insertions, and contradictory character behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Fluency test judging the pacing of the narrative (how events unfold over time and whether pacing supports engagement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert anti-patterns: stories that spiral into repetitive patterns, or that rapidly accelerate through time after an initial scene leading to absurd/fragmented progression. Passing requires balanced pacing that maintains interest and logical progression; failure shown by sudden time leaps, repetitive loops, or uncontrolled acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene vs Exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Fluency test evaluating the balance between showing (scenes) and telling (exposition/summary) in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts noted AI/higher-poor-quality writing often shows predictable formations: strong topic sentences at paragraph starts and summary sentences at the end. Passing favors vivid scenes and embodied moments; failing is overly expositional, summary-heavy prose, and reliance on tell-not-show patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary Devices & Language Proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A Fluency (Literary Devices & Language) test assessing effective, meaningful use of figurative language, metaphors, diction, and general language proficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures include abstruse or incoherent metaphors that add no meaning, superficial ornamental figurative language, clichéd/simplistic metaphors, repetitive 'pet phrases' across stories (e.g., 'inky sky', 'tendrils', 'etched'), and unusual/inconsistent syntax. Passing requires figurative language that adds meaning and texture, varied diction, and syntactic appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: A Fluency test judging whether the story arrives at a satisfying and purposeful ending (closure, resolution or intentional open-ness appropriate to the piece).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts observed AI often 'doesn't know how to end'—forestalling endings by expanding scope, producing multiple disparate endings, plateauing falling action, or leaving characters behind. Passing requires endings that feel purposeful to the narrative; failure includes abrupt, unfocused, or endlessly dilating conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A Flexibility test assessing the story's ability to navigate, vary, and handle emotions in nuanced ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passing indicates the work can shift emotional tones appropriately and support emotional complexity; failure manifests as flat, unvaried emotional expression or mismatched/unsupportive emotional shifts. (Text references Flexibility dimension assessing emotional range; experts used this lens when differentiating AI vs human output.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective & Voice Flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A Flexibility test evaluating diversity and appropriateness of narrative perspectives and the consistency/adaptability of voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passing favors deliberate choices of perspective and voice, including effective shifts where appropriate; failing includes rigid, monocular perspective or awkward/unmotivated voice shifts. TTCW notes this dimension values diverse narrative perspectives but may disfavour single-viewpoint works depending on panel bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural Flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A Flexibility test assessing how the story experiments with, balances, or departs from conventional narrative structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passing entails purposeful structural variation that serves the story; failures include structural choices that disrupt readability without artistic justification. The paper cautions that Fluency/Flexibility tests may penalize experimental works that intentionally blend techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality in Form
rubrics_metrics.description: An Originality test assessing innovation at the formal/structural level (novel forms, arrangements, or presentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passing requires noticeable formal innovation; failing includes reliance on well-worn forms or mechanical re-use of tropes. Authors note TTCW Originality3 rewards formal innovation but may underrate creativity within strict formal boundaries (e.g., mythic structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality in Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: An Originality test assessing novelty of ideas, insights, and conceptual content in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passing signals fresh, unexpected ideas or perspectives; failing is predictable, derivative, or telegraphed thinking. Experts found some models produced low originality in thought compared to humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality in Theme & Content
rubrics_metrics.description: An Originality test evaluating uniqueness of themes, subject matter, and content choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passing implies uncommon or inventive themes and content combinations; failing involves clichéd themes, recycled tropes, or content that feels generic. The paper notes LLM outputs often revert to tropes and repetition, lowering theme/content originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: World Building & Setting
rubrics_metrics.description: An Elaboration test assessing the richness and sensory grounding of setting and world-building elements (e.g., elements that appeal to the five senses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts asked to list 'elements in the story that call to each of the five senses' as part of evaluation. Passing requires tangible, evocative setting details integrated into the narrative; failing includes thin, generic, repetitive, or nonsensical setting descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Development
rubrics_metrics.description: An Elaboration test assessing whether characters are developed, motivated, and have narrative impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures observed: characters appearing without warning and disappearing without impact, contradictory actions, lack of arc or motivation. Passing requires consistent, meaningful character actions and development that influence the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical Complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: An Elaboration test assessing the presence of subtext, implication, and rhetorical subtlety (as opposed to purely literal/expositional writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts highlighted lack of subtext as an AI weakness—dialogue that over-explains, direct exposition replacing implication, and absence of implied meaning or relational subtext. Passing requires layered meaning, subtext, and rhetorical nuance; failing is literal, expository, or unnaturally 'hackish' dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary judgment + Justification protocol (TTCW annotation format)
rubrics_metrics.description: How each TTCW test is administered: binary (Yes/No) judgments by experts accompanied by a justification paragraph explaining the assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts produced binary labels and a justification paragraph. For LLM-based assessment, prompts asked the model to list elements relevant to the test (e.g., sensory elements for world-building), provide reasoning (chain-of-thought style), then answer Yes/No. The paper reports that expert justifications were concise and thematic; LLM explanations were procedural and often longer. Agreement measured against majority expert vote (Cohen's Kappa).

rubrics_metrics.name: TTCW administration with LLM assessors (implementation guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural guidance for having LLMs act as assessors of TTCW tests (prompt design and expected behaviors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompts provided: (1) the story, (2) expanded TTCW context, (3) the TTCW question, (4) an instruction guiding chain-of-thought reasoning. The LLM is asked to first list elements relevant to the test, then decide Yes/No with reasoning. The authors note zero-shot prompting was used (and few-shot was tested without significant gains), and chain-of-thought improved LLM explanations but did not yield positive correlation with experts for most tests. This is an operational rubric for automated TTCW deployment rather than a quality metric of stories.
